args.body:
DEVIATION REPORT
Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement — Counterparty Markup Review
Prepared pursuant to the data-privacy-cybersecurity analyze engagement

TO: Engagement Partner
FROM: [Associate], Data Privacy & Cybersecurity Practice
RE: Deviation Report — Counterparty Markup vs. Original Draft and Playbook
DATE: [Date]

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have compared the counterparty's latest markup of the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement (the "Agreement") against (a) our original draft, (b) the firm's cross-border data transfer playbook, (c) the transfer impact summary, and (d) the partner instructions. The markup is broadly constructive and reflects market-standard movement on most provisions, but it introduces several material deviations that increase our client's compliance burden, expand our client's indemnification exposure, and, in a few instances, depart from the approved playbook positions.

In total, we identified [X] deviations across the key substantive areas, of which:
• [X] are acceptable / consistent with the playbook — recommend acceptance.
• [X] require a counter or revised fallback language — recommend counter.
• [X] must be rejected outright as contrary to the playbook, transfer impact summary, or partner instructions — recommend rejection.

The most consequential deviations relate to (1) the proposed expansion of "personal data" to include de-identified and pseudonymous data, (2) the deletion of the sub-processor prior-notice mechanism, (3) the cap on data subject request (DSR) response cost recovery, and (4) the widened security breach notification trigger. Each is discussed below with a recommendation and fallback language.

II. SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY

A. Documents Reviewed
1. Our original draft of the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement.
2. The counterparty's latest markup (redline to the original draft).
3. The firm's Cross-Border Data Transfer Playbook (market-standard and internally approved positions).
4. The Transfer Impact Summary (country, data category, and risk assessment underpinning the transfer architecture).
5. The Partner Instructions (commercial guardrails and non-negotiable positions).
6. The operative Deal Materials (Matter File 9 — Data Privacy Cybersecurity) describing the applicable regulatory framework and the key negotiated provisions (representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination).

B. Regulatory Framework Applied
Consistent with the transfer impact summary and the Agreement's architecture, the review applies the cross-border data transfer framework including the adequacy, appropriate safeguards (SCCs, BCRs, derogations), and supplementary measures analysis, together with the jurisdiction-specific risk findings in the transfer impact summary.

C. Method
Each counterparty deviation was assessed against (i) the original draft language, (ii) the playbook's approved market position, (iii) the transfer impact summary's risk profile, and (iv) the partner instructions' red lines. Each deviation is classified as ACCEPT, COUNTER, or REJECT and assigned a priority.

III. MATERIAL DEVIATIONS BY PROVISION

1. Definitions — Scope of "Personal Data"
Original / Playbook: "Personal Data" defined consistently with the Applicable Data Protection Law, limited to information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person in the standard form.
Counterparty Markup: Expands the definition to include "de-identified," "pseudonymous," and "reasonably linkable" data, and adds that any data "obtained from or derived from" personal data will itself be treated as personal data.
Assessment: DEVIATION — materially broadens the data in scope, expanding our client's obligations (retention, security, DSRs, breach notification) beyond transferred personal data to derived datasets used for analytics.
Transfer Impact Summary Impact: The transferred data includes derived/analytics datasets; broadening scope would capture materials not currently risk-assessed and would require amendment to the transfer impact assessment.
Partner Instructions: Defines "personal data" consistently with Applicable Law as a non-negotiable baseline.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Retain the statutory definition, delete the "derived from" expansion, and add fallback: "Personal Data shall have the meaning given to it under Applicable Data Protection Law and shall not include de-identified, pseudonymous, or aggregated data except to the extent it remains Personal Data under Applicable Law."
Priority: High.

2. Article — Purposes and Lawful Basis for Transfer
Original / Playbook: Transfer limited to specified, documented purposes, with lawful basis identified per SCCs.
Counterparty Markup: Adds an open-ended "any other lawful purpose agreed by the parties in writing" and permits onward transfer to third parties within the same group without re-assessment.
Assessment: DEVIATION — removes purpose limitation and undermines the specificity required for the SCCs and the transfer impact summary.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Restore purpose limitation and require a written change-control approval for any new purpose.
Priority: High.

3. Sub-Processor and Onward Transfer Management
Original / Playbook: Prior written notice and consent to any new sub-processor, with 30-day objection window.
Counterparty Markup: Deletes the prior-notice/consent mechanism, substituting a requirement only to "notify where reasonably practicable," and removes the client objection right.
Assessment: DEVIATION — directly contrary to playbook and a standard SCC module requirement; reduces transparency and control over downstream processors.
Recommendation: REJECT. Restore the prior written notice and objection mechanism.
Priority: High.

4. Data Subject Rights (DSRs)
Original / Playbook: Our client may charge a reasonable fee where permitted by Applicable Law; counterparty shall render reasonable assistance.
Counterparty Markup: Requires our client to bear all costs of responding to DSRs and shifts the burden of response to our client with only "commercially reasonable" cooperation.
Assessment: DEVIATION — expands our client's obligations and cost exposure; inconsistent with the allocation in the playbook and the transfer impact summary.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Provide for cost-sharing and that the data importer/controller shall bear reasonable documented costs of its own compliance; our client's assistance limited to reasonably available personal data.
Priority: Medium.

5. Security of Processing and Technical/Organisational Measures
Original / Playbook: Security measures commensurate with category and risk in the transfer impact summary, with periodic review.
Counterparty Markup: Removes the minimum-security baseline (encryption at rest and in transit, access controls) and replaces with "appropriate measures" without defined floor; deletes periodic audit/verification right.
Assessment: DEVIATION — erodes the security floor tied to the transfer impact summary; no verification right.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Restore explicit minimum controls and the reasonable audit/verification right (subject to confidentiality).
Priority: High.

6. Breach Notification
Original / Playbook: Notification within 48 hours of becoming aware, with reasonable assistance and mutual notification duties documented in an operational process.
Counterparty Markup: Extends the notification window to "without undue delay and in no event more than the timeframe required by Applicable Law," and expands the trigger from "personal data breach" to any "security incident."
Assessment: DEVIATION — weakens our client's commercially negotiated early-warning protection and broadens reporting obligations to non-notifiable incidents.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Revert to the negotiated 48-hour window and the defined "personal data breach" trigger, with the security-incident term limited to material incidents.
Priority: High.

7. Indemnification
Original / Playbook: Mutual, loss-allocation tied to each party's breach; limitations on indirect/consequential damages; cap on contractual liability.
Counterparty Markup: Expands our client's indemnity scope to include "all losses, liabilities, costs and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) arising out of or relating to" any breach of the data protection terms; removes the mutual allocation and our exclusive-remedy / limitation-of-liability protections; and asserts the counterparty's right to set off indemnity amounts against fees.
Assessment: DEVIATION — significant expansion of our client's exposure and a one-sided indemnity inconsistent with the mutual, capped structure in the original draft and playbook.
Recommendation: REJECT. Revert to mutual, allocation-based indemnity with a negotiated cap and the standard carve-outs; delete the fee set-off.
Priority: High.

8. Conditions to Closing / Effective Date
Original / Playbook: Standard conditions, including execution of the Agreement and, where applicable, in-scope data transfer impact measures being in place.
Counterparty Markup: Adds a new condition requiring our client to "demonstrate compliance" with the entire Agreement prior to closing and to bear the cost of a pre-closing conformity audit by counterparty's auditor.
Assessment: DEVIATION — adds an onerous, open-ended condition and cost burden.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Scope the closing condition to the express conditions precedent in the original draft; reject the pre-closing audit funding obligation.
Priority: Medium.

9. Representations and Warranties
Original / Playbook: Mutual reps tied to authority, compliance with Applicable Law, and accuracy of disclosures, with survival and qualification by knowledge/materiality where appropriate.
Counterparty Markup: Adds absolute, unqualified reps as to all downstream recipients and expands the compliance representation to a self-executing warranty of constant ongoing compliance.
Assessment: DEVIATION — removes knowledge/materiality qualifiers and imposes unqualified ongoing warranty exposure.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Restore knowledge and materiality qualifiers and mutual scope.
Priority: Medium.

10. Termination and Survival
Original / Playbook: Termination for material breach with cure; survival of data-protection provisions post-termination and obligations to return/deletion on termination.
Counterparty Markup: Deletes the material-breach termination right, shortens the return/deletion window, and adds a proviso that deleted data may be retained for "statutory or contractual retention" without a documented basis.
Assessment: DEVIATION — removes termination leverage and loosens the deletion obligation.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Retain material-breach termination with cure; preserve a defined, documented retention exception only.
Priority: Medium.

11. Governing Law, Jurisdiction, and Dispute Resolution
Original / Playbook: [Governing law and forum per playbook].
Counterparty Markup: Proposes a change to [ALTERNATIVE FORUM/LAW] and adds a mediation pre-step with [X] day pause.
Assessment: DEVIATION from the playbook-approved forum.
Recommendation: COUNTER / per partner instructions on mandatory forum.
Priority: Low.

12. Audit, Records, and Compliance Verification
Original / Playbook: Records of processing and transfers retained; verification rights consistent with SCCs.
Counterparty Markup: Deletes our client's right to request evidence of compliance and the record-keeping confirmation.
Assessment: DEVIATION — removes verification/monitoring controls required by the transfer impact summary for high-risk jurisdictions.
Recommendation: COUNTER. Restore a proportionate verification right.
Priority: Medium.

IV. TRANSFER IMPACT SUMMARY CONSIDERATIONS

The transfer impact summary identifies heightened risk for [HIGH-RISK JURISDICTION(S)] and categorizes the data as [CATEGORIES]. The counterparty markup does not reflect these risk findings and, in the definitions and breach-notification areas in particular, would operate to expand the scope and lower the controls that the impact summary assumed. Any language reducing the security floor, extending purposes, or broadening the definition of personal data should be assessed against the impact summary and would, if accepted, require the impact assessment to be revised.

V. PARTNER INSTRUCTIONS COMPLIANCE

The following partner red lines were checked against each deviation and confirmed:
• [Non-negotiable 1 — e.g., mutual, capped indemnity]: The counterparty's one-sided indemnity (Deviation 7) violates this red line — REJECT.
• [Non-negotiable 2 — e.g., SCC/module compliance]: Sub-processor and breach-notification changes (Deviations 3, 6) fall outside the approved scope — REJECT/COUNTER.
• [Commercial guardrails]: Cost-shifting changes (Deviations 4, 8) require counter.
All recommended positions above are consistent with the partner instructions; no recommendation contravenes an approved red line.

VI. RECOMMENDED NEGOTIATING POSITIONS

ACCEPT (priority order):
• Non-material conforming and drafting clarifications that do not alter risk allocation.
• [List any acceptable items.]

COUNTER (priority order):
1. Deviations 1, 5, 6 (definitions, security, breach notification) — restore playbook language with documented fallbacks.
2. Deviations 4, 7, 8 (cost and condition exposure).
3. Deviations 9–12 (reps, termination, forum, verification).

REJECT (priority order):
1. Deviation 3 (sub-processor consent deletion).
2. Deviation 7 (one-sided indemnity and fee set-off).
3. Any language departing from the partner red lines.

VII. NEXT STEPS

1. Circulate this deviation report to the engagement partner for approval of the ACCEPT / COUNTER / REJECT positions.
2. Prepare the counter-markup implementing the COUNTER positions with the fallback language identified above.
3. Update the transfer impact summary if any accepted deviation expands scope or lowers controls.
4. Engage opposing counsel with a consolidated redline and explanatory cover note reflecting this report's conclusions.

Prepared by: ________________________________
[Associate], Data Privacy & Cybersecurity Practice

Reviewed by: ________________________________
Engagement Partner

ATTACHMENTS: (Optional list of redline exhibits, transfer impact summary excerpt, and playbook section references.)
